title: Mindful Access: Why Equitable Technology Use in Schools Can’t Be Optional
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Marcinek argues that equity in school technology is about more than handing out devices: unequal home access produces unequal habits, and schools are often the only place students can learn purposeful digital use. Drawing on his book Teaching Digital Kindness and a podcast guest, he frames technology use as a social skill that must be taught with guidance and modelling. He closes with a direct call to school leaders to design equitable access and support systems rather than assume a level playing field. The piece is partly a plug for his own book and podcast, but the school-policy argument is substantive.
points: A one-to-one device program does not guarantee equitable opportunity unless access is paired with guidance and scaffolding.
Where home technology means unsupervised scrolling, students default to entertainment, so schools must rewrite that script.
Technology use is a social and relational skill shaped by community expectations, not merely a technical one.
Mindful integration asks whether a tool deepens learning, whether students reflect on their use, and whether adults model digital kindness.
School leaders set the tone; equity in technology use happens by design, through systems and not just purchases.
quotes: When we talk about technology in schools, the conversation often skips straight to the tools: the new devices, the latest apps, the emerging AI platforms. But beneath the devices and software lies something far more critical: access. And without equitable access, we’re not just creating digital divides—we’re reinforcing them.

We cannot assume that every student’s home environment supports healthy technology habits. If students only encounter structured, intentional technology use within the walls of our schools, then schools become the only place where these digital skills can develop. Without that support, inequitable access leads to problematic use: students may rely on devices solely for entertainment or distraction rather than learning, connection, or creation.

This is why we need to stop assuming a level playing field when it comes to technology access. A one-to-one device program does not automatically mean equitable opportunity. Simply handing out devices is not enough. We need to pair access with guidance, scaffolding, and opportunities for students to practice mindful use of technology under the care of educators who model digital kindness, responsibility, and balance.

Schools have a responsibility to rewrite that script. We must create intentional, supported spaces where students learn to research, collaborate, create, and communicate online with purpose. This isn’t just a “nice to have”—it’s an urgent equity issue.
As school leaders, we set the tone. Equity in technology use doesn’t happen by chance; it happens by design.
We cannot assume technology access at home looks like it does at school. We cannot assume support structures exist outside our buildings.
